built_with_verified.value: declared by the authors (25): ai-agents, cloud-firestore, express.js, firebase, firebase-authentication, firebase-cloud-functions, firebase-hosting, gemini-api · no repository published, so these are the team's own claim and nothing corroborates them

clone_cost.note: our estimate with assumptions visible; not a claim about the team

assumptions: an acceptance standard per workflow, written down before shipping, because nothing in the capture defines what a good generated asset is and without one 'quality' is unfalsifiable
a cost model per generation (tokens, seconds of video, retries) priced against $49/month before adding any video-heavy workflow, since the page never publishes one
distribution assumed to be the hard part: the record's own growth was founder-led and organic, so a clone inherits the product and not the 13 customers
brand-context persistence (logos, headshots, style) needs a store and a review path if outputs are to be reusable rather than regenerated
value.estimate: 3-4 weeks per workflow a business would actually pay for, and the ninth is not nine times cheaper than the first
value.why: The generation plumbing is commodity: Gemini text and image endpoints, Veo for video, TTS for voiceover, Search grounding for the digest, all of it behind Cloud Functions and Cloud Tasks with Firestore for job state - a small team can stand up two or three of these in a month, and the page says its own build was substantially done with Gemini coding agents and Antigravity, which is a claim about speed of authoring, not about defensibility. What is not commodity is the per-vertical taste that makes each output acceptable - what a staged living room has to look like for a listing agent to send it, how a menu photo has to be lit - plus auth, billing, analytics and the trust required for a business to hand a workspace its brand. And the acquisition story the record actually claims as its accomplishment is founder-led outreach at $0 spend, which cannot be cloned at all: the moat named in the page is the team's ability to sell to SMBs, not the pipeline.

data_and_models.value: No model is trained and none is claimed to be. The system is an orchestration layer over vendor capabilities: Gemini APIs across text generation and analysis, image generation and editing, video, speech and Google Search-grounded intelligence, with Veo and gemini-tts named in the tag list as the specific generators. On the serving side it is Firebase Cloud Functions plus Cloud Tasks for asynchronous generation, Firestore and Cloud Storage for job state and produced assets, Secret Manager for credentials, Firebase hosting, auth, logging and analytics, with React and Node/Express at the edge. The authored content is notable for what it does not say: no model version is named for any of the five capability classes, no routing rule is given for which workflow calls which model, and no per-generation cost, latency or failure rate is published - which matters because the page itself explains that some operations are computationally intensive and asynchronous, so those three quantities are the product's real economic constraints.

how_it_works.value: Built 'AI-native from day one', beginning as workflow prototypes in Google AI Studio. The page credits Gemini-powered coding agents and Google Antigravity for architecture brainstorming, coding, testing, debugging and iteration, and Google Stitch for the frontend design process. In production the shape is an asynchronous architecture for AI workloads: Firebase Cloud Functions and Cloud Tasks orchestrate generation jobs, while Firestore and Cloud Storage hold job state and generated assets, on top of the authentication, logging and analytics that Firebase and Google Cloud provide. Model use is spread across capability classes rather than one endpoint - Gemini APIs for text generation and analysis, image generation and editing, video, speech, and Google Search-grounded intelligence - with Node/Express and React at the edges and the twenty-five-item Built With list also naming Veo, gemini-tts, Secret Manager and serverless. AI is also used internally: market analysis, customer targeting, UX development, debugging and documentation.

how_they_tested.value: Nothing is measured in the sense this catalog counts as measurement. There is no test suite, no eval, no accuracy, acceptance or rejection-rate figure, and no quality claim for any of the nine workflows - no statement, for instance, of how often a generated virtual-staged room or product video is acceptable to the business that asked for it. What the page offers instead is usage: 'early customer usage has been important in helping us make those decisions' between impressive-sounding and genuinely valuable features, which is product research rather than a test result, and 13 businesses as the population it was gathered from, unpublished per workflow. The one appearance of the word testing is in the description of how the code was written - Gemini-powered coding agents and Antigravity used for 'architecture brainstorming, coding, testing, debugging and iteration' - so the assertion is that testing happened, with no harness, count or result attached and no repository to read it from. The absence is load-bearing for a claim of this shape: the acceptance rate of a generated marketing image is the number a buyer of this product would need.

limits_they_disclosed.value: Three, and all three are stated as product restraint rather than technical failure. The first is 'avoiding the temptation to simply put powerful AI models behind generic prompt boxes' - owners want an outcome, so the workflows are organised around what the business is trying to accomplish, with most prompting and model complexity abstracted behind the experience. The second is workload heterogeneity: text, image, video and research jobs differ by orders of magnitude in cost, some completing quickly while others are computationally intensive and asynchronous, and the Cloud Tasks plus Firebase layer is what keeps that invisible to the user. The third is described as a continual judgement call between features that are technically impressive and features that create genuine value, with early customer usage cited as the thing that decided it.

The gallery carries one screenshot per workflow, which is corroboration of existence and not of quality - and note that breadth of this kind is itself a claim about maintenance cost per workflow, which the page never addresses

what_breaks_first.value: Unit economics on the expensive workflows, then the quality question nobody measured. A $49/month plan is priced against a catalogue that includes Veo-class video generation and image editing for every customer; one realtor rendering a dozen listings a week can out-earn the subscription in inference on its own, and the page publishes no per-generation cost, latency or failure rate - while simultaneously admitting that some operations are computationally intensive and asynchronous, i.e. it knows exactly where the exposure is. Second: nine workflows means nine vendor surfaces, each with its own silent quality drift, and there is no acceptance metric for any of them, so a model version bump changes what a customer receives with nothing in the loop to notice. Third: '13 businesses using it' has no denominator - not paying, not retained, not per-workflow - so the traction claim that carries the record cannot be turned into a rate by a reader at all.

what_it_does.value: attainDesk turns common small-business needs into guided, business-specific AI workflows from one workspace: create social-media content; virtually stage real-estate listings; turn property images into video tours; create short promotional product videos; transform ordinary food photos into polished menu and marketing images; generate business logos; create professional headshots; generate branded meeting backgrounds; and a Daily Digest that surfaces relevant market developments, local business groups, events and opportunities. The named verticals are real estate, food, manufacturing, construction, education, clothing and professional services. The features differ and the goal is stated as one: help a small business understand its market, present itself professionally, reach customers and grow without needing a large specialist team.

what_it_is.value: An AI-native operations workspace for small businesses, where each business outcome - virtual staging a listing, turning food photos into menu images, a product video, a logo, a headshot, a Daily Digest of local opportunities - is its own guided workflow over an asynchronous Firebase Cloud Functions and Cloud Tasks generation pipeline, on the stated premise that owners should not have to learn AI to put it to work.

what_to_steal.value: Refuse the prompt box. The stated design principle - users describe a business outcome while model selection, prompting, context and iteration happen behind the scenes - is transferable to any vertical agent, and the async plumbing that makes it survivable is the second half: Cloud Functions plus Cloud Tasks so a two-second text job and a two-minute video job share one UI contract with Firestore holding job state. Then steal the honesty of the product framing itself: 'the best AI experience can sometimes feel like there is less AI, not more' is the line to put on a wall in any team shipping a model-backed workflow, and the Digest-that-found-the-first-customer loop is a template for pointing your own research surface at your own acquisition problem.

The category is crowded here and elsewhere: Reeloli, Small Business AI Growth Desk and VibeMarketer are in this corpus with the same 'SMBs, no prompting, we do the marketing' pitch, so the wedge is execution, not insight. And nothing about the nine workflows is measured - no acceptance rate, no per-generation cost, no quality claim, no repository - so the record can support 'this team shipped a business' but not 'this mechanism works'. Breadth is also unpriced: nine generation pipelines is a maintenance commitment the page never accounts for.

built_with_verified.value: declared by the authors (20): clickhouse, cloud-run, cloud-storage, docker, fastapi, ffmpeg, firestore, gemini · no repository published, so these are the team's own claim and nothing corroborates them

clone_cost.note: our estimate with assumptions visible; not a claim about the team

assumptions: assume 1 engineer + 1 designer, 6 weeks, and real spend money for the generation ladder (their full film priced ~$238)
you can start smaller: one shot class, one priced gate, one table of verdicts — the calibration view is what takes the weeks
the character-reference locking is the part that needs image-model skill, not plumbing
value.why: the agent choreography is a weekend; the honest parts are the ledger, the calibration views, and the locked-identity image pipeline

data_and_models.value: Model choice is per task shape across the Gemini family on Vertex AI (Pro for whole-script reasoning, Flash for rule-bound generation, Flash-Lite for batch); data is the team's own generation ledger in ClickHouse (shot class, parameters, tier, attempt number, keep/again, cost, duration, model) feeding two materialised views for pass rates and prediction calibration; Firestore holds state, Cloud Storage holds media.

how_it_works.value: One Cloud Run service shipping frontend and backend together; Gemini family on Vertex AI; Firestore for state; Cloud Storage for media; ClickHouse for the learning loop reached through the official mcp-clickhouse server. Model assignment is a cost decision by shape of work: Pro holds the whole screenplay in mind at once (37 scenes to chapters, resolving that 'Luna' and '月音' are the same character), Flash does rule-bound work (prompt writing, subtitle translation, counting people in a finished clip), Flash-Lite does high-volume low-judgement batches. Screenplay parsing keeps the expensive model because it is the foundation: the premium is ~$0.11 on a 90-page script and an error there propagates invisibly. Money gates are schema state transitions, never prompt instructions, because a probabilistic component cannot guarantee a hard requirement.

how_they_tested.value: No test suite is published; the evidence offered is an A/B measurement (29%→49% on the same shots), a seeded deliberate ×0.92 bias in the ledger to prove the calibration view catches optimism, and stated per-shot outcome logging.

limits_they_disclosed.value: $150 of credits against $1 per ten seconds of footage meant no 'just generate it again'; the full film prices near $238 and is still unshot. In production debugging: a 200 response with a 30 MB file and no burned-in subtitles, because the container had no fonts and ffmpeg exits 0 regardless; a 300 s video timeout that never fired because requests measures the gap between reads, so the platform killed it at 900 s and the failure record was lost with it; a health endpoint that reported '12 fonts, 4 CJK' while fontconfig's config file was missing, i.e. a check that looked like verification and was not; two copies of the same learning-loop component drifting, one reading the wrong key and quietly showing 0 for three days. Adopted rules: degrading is fine, degrading silently is not; demo build and production build are one image, one commit, differing only by an env var.

what_breaks_first.value: The success-rate estimate. Below a few hundred logged shots per shot class the displayed percentage is a prior wearing a lab coat, so build the calibration view (predicted vs observed) in week one or you are shipping confidence theatre. Second to break: prompt-injection-free subtitle burn-in on a fresh container, which is exactly the bug they documented (ffmpeg exits 0 with no fonts).

what_it_does.value: User drops a screenplay. The system reads it whole, splits it into chapters, breaks chapters into shots, casts characters, writes prompts, generates footage, then inspects what it made: if shot 3 contains a person who should not be there it notices and folds that into the retry instruction. The user presses keep or again. Before any spend it quotes odds: this chapter is 12 shots, ~$4.50, about half will pass first try. Casting is a hard gate; a character reference costs $0.02 while a shot costs $1 and a finished segment ~$20, so every decision is pushed down the cost ladder. Face is an input, look is an output: an uploaded photo is locked as identity while only the style re-renders, and wardrobe is per chapter. Style buttons carry their own success adjustment (photorealistic −10pt vs animation +12/+15pt). Every generation and every keep/again verdict is written to ClickHouse, so once enough similar shots exist the estimate switches from built-in priors to that user's own numbers and says which one you are looking at plus the sample size. After casting, every prompt is exportable.

what_it_is.value: Drop a screenplay; nine agents read it, cast it, price it, shoot it, and watch what they made — with the quote shown before you press the button.

what_to_steal.value: Two moves, and they compose: (1) quote the cost and the pass rate before the button, and push every hesitation down the price ladder (settle a character at $0.02, not $1); (2) log every verdict row into a store you can query, then let the estimate switch from your priors to the user's own measured numbers and label which one they are reading, with sample size. Also steal 'the money gate is a schema transition, not a prompt'.

greenlight-nine-agent-production-crew.name: Greenlight - Nine-Agent Production Crew
verdict_reasons: reads strong, but only 64% of the rubric was checkable (no public artifact to read) → caveats, not strong
greenlight-nine-agent-production-crew.worth_note: The wedge is not 'AI video' — it is pricing a generation step before you commit and then making your own logged outcomes the estimator. That transfers to anything with an expensive call (image gen, agent runs, transcription at volume). Not 'breakthrough' only because it ships as one team's v1 with no public code to adopt.
